Modelers compare geometry, properties, and standards by hand. Estimators need the same information for a reliable handoff.
textPreview: Review happens across | separate tools |  | Modelers compare geometry, properties, and standards by hand. Estimators need the same inform...

text: Pain points, 35 seconds. A visually convincing building model can still contain missing or mismatched classifications. Reviewers need to reconcile object identity, location, and the standard reference. Explain these as target user problems, not measured error rates. Estimators depend on consistent element categories for downstream work. Sources: user project brief; ASTM-UniFormat.xlsx Instructions A2 and ASTM 2015 A7:H7.

text: Solution, 35 seconds. The Excel file is a classification database. It contains Instructions, ASTM 1997 and ASTM 2015 sheets. Use one reference edition consistently. Automated classification comparisons and write-back are development targets. Geometry, context and properties help distinguish similar categories, such as interior and exterior doors. The workbook does not itself provide dimensional, fire-safety or accessibility requirements. Source: assets/ASTM-UniFormat.xlsx.

alt: User-supplied architectural classification example showing a window mislabeled as exterior walls and a suggested exterior-window classification

text: Main example, 45 seconds. The selected object is an exterior window. In this illustrative scenario its model label is B2010, Exterior Walls. The workbook lists B2020, Exterior Windows, on ASTM 2015 row 195. Forma is intended to present the mismatch and propose a classification for designer review. This image is supplied by the user and represents a concept, not a detected issue in the sample IFC. Source: ASTM-UniFormat.xlsx ASTM 2015 A186:B186 and A195:B195; user-supplied visual. Classification consistency does not establish building-code safety compliance.
